present-day-dimensionless-density-parame.intuitive_summary: It represents the fraction of the universe's total energy budget currently supplied by a specific ingredient, evaluated against the precise threshold required to make spatial geometry flat today.

determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.title: Determinant of the Jacobian Matrix
determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.description: Quantifies the local volume scaling factor and orientation change induced by a smooth coordinate transformation or differentiable mapping between manifolds.
determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.conceptual_definition: Given a differentiable vector-valued map $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, the Jacobian matrix $\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}} = \mathbf{J}$ consists of the partial derivatives $J_{ij} = \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}$. Its determinant, $J = \det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}})$, governs the transformation of differential volume elements via $d^n\mathbf{y} = |\det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}})| \, d^n\mathbf{x}$ and appears as the metric volume factor in continuum mechanics, field theories, and canonical transformations.
determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.interpretation: The symbol $\text{Det}(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}})$ denotes the determinant of the $n \times n$ first-order partial derivative matrix $\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}}$. A value where $\det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}}) > 0$ indicates a local preservation of spatial orientation, whereas $\det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}}) < 0$ implies an orientation reversal (reflection). In Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations strictly enforce $\det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}}) = 1$, preserving invariant phase-space volume as dictated by Liouville's theorem.
determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.limits_and_boundary: When $\det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}}) = 0$, the mapping is locally non-invertible, indicating a coordinate singularity, caustic, or critical point. For an identity transformation $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}} = \mathbb{I}$ and $\det(\mathbf{M}_{\text{Jacobian}}) = 1$.
determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.symmetry_origin: Diffeomorphism invariance and general coordinate covariance on smooth differentiable manifolds.

\\text{Det}.name: determinant operator
\\text{Det}.description: Matrix determinant mapping an $n \times n$ linear operator to a scalar value representing hypervolume scaling.

\\mathbf{M}_{Jacobian}.name: Jacobian matrix
\\mathbf{M}_{Jacobian}.description: Matrix of first-order partial derivatives representing the local linear approximation of a multivariable vector transformation.

determinant-of-jacobian-matrix-e54fbf3e.intuitive_summary: The Jacobian determinant measures how much an infinitesimal geometric box expands, shrinks, or flips its orientation when deformed or mapped into new coordinates.

kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.title: Double Classical Kinetic Energy in Terms of Momentum
kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.description: Represents the dynamic quantity $p^2/m$, which is equal to twice the non-relativistic kinetic energy of a classical point mass or particle, expressed via momentum and mass.
kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.conceptual_definition: In classical Newtonian mechanics, the quantity $\frac{p^2}{m}$ characterizes the ratio of the squared linear momentum $p^2 = (mv)^2$ to inertial mass $m$. It is identically equal to $2E_k$, where $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is the standard non-relativistic kinetic energy, serving as a core scaling term in Hamiltonian mechanics and quantum mechanical operators.
kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.interpretation: The expression $\frac{p^2}{m}$ directly arises by eliminating velocity $v$ from the definition of linear momentum $p = mv$ and evaluating $v^2 = \frac{p^2}{m^2}$. Here, $p$ denotes the magnitude of the canonical or linear momentum, and $m$ represents the invariant or rest mass of the particle. Half of this quantity represents the standard non-relativistic kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, while $\frac{p^2}{m}$ represents the full coefficient appearing in the virial theorem and quadratic kinetic Hamiltonians.
kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit $v \ll c$, the expression relates directly to kinetic energy. As $v \to c$, the relativistic mass-energy relation $E = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4}$ replaces this classical quadratic term. When $p \to 0$, the quantity approaches $0$.
kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation invariance via Noether's theorem implies conservation of linear momentum $\mathbf{p}$, which determines the conserved dynamical quantities governed by kinetic terms like $p^2/m$.

p.name: linear momentum
p.description: Magnitude of the linear momentum of the particle

kinetic-energy-from-momentum-and-mass-39.intuitive_summary: Measures twice the energy of motion stored in a body by combining its momentum and mass, scaling quadratically with motion.

ratio-of-present-to-past-cosmic-scale-fa.title: Ratio of Present to Past Cosmic Scale Factor
ratio-of-present-to-past-cosmic-scale-fa.description: This equation represents the ratio of the cosmic scale factor at the present epoch to the scale factor at an earlier time t.
ratio-of-present-to-past-cosmic-scale-fa.conceptual_definition: In the context of an expanding universe, the cosmic scale factor $a(t)$ quantifies the relative expansion or contraction of space over time. This specific ratio compares the size of the universe today, denoted by $a_0$, to its size at a particular past moment $t$, denoted by $a(t)$.
ratio-of-present-to-past-cosmic-scale-fa.interpretation: The value of this ratio directly indicates how much the universe has expanded between the past time $t$ and the present day. A value greater than 1 signifies expansion, meaning the universe was smaller at time $t$ than it is now. This ratio is a fundamental component of the cosmological redshift relation, where $1 + z = a_0 / a(t)$, linking the observed redshift of light from distant objects to the expansion history of the universe.
ratio-of-present-to-past-cosmic-scale-fa.limits_and_boundary: The scale factor $a(t)$ is always a positive value. At the present epoch, $t = t_0$, $a(t_0) = a_0$, making the ratio equal to 1. As one considers earlier times approaching the Big Bang ($t \to 0$), $a(t)$ approaches 0, causing the ratio to approach infinity. Conversely, for future times, if the universe continues to expand, $a(t)$ will increase, and the ratio $a_0 / a(t)$ will approach 0.
ratio-of-present-to-past-cosmic-scale-fa.symmetry_origin: While this ratio itself is a mathematical construct, the underlying scale factor $a(t)$ is derived from the Friedmann equations. These equations are a direct consequence of applying Einstein's field equations to a universe that is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic on large scales, a principle known as the cosmological principle, which embodies spatial symmetries.

a_0.name: a_0
a_0.description: The cosmic scale factor at the present epoch (t=t_0), representing the current relative size of the universe. It is a dimensionless quantity, often normalized such that $a_0 = 1$.

a(t).name: a(t)
a(t).description: The cosmic scale factor at a specific past time $t$, representing the relative size of the universe at that epoch. It is a dimensionless quantity, typically normalized such that $a_0 = 1$.

photon-momentum-wavelength-relation-de8f.title: Photon Momentum-Wavelength Relation
photon-momentum-wavelength-relation-de8f.description: This equation establishes the fundamental relationship between the momentum of a photon and its wavelength, incorporating Planck's constant.
photon-momentum-wavelength-relation-de8f.conceptual_definition: The momentum of a photon, a massless particle of light, is inversely proportional to its wavelength. This relationship is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, demonstrating the wave-particle duality of light where both wave-like properties (wavelength) and particle-like properties (momentum) are intrinsically linked. It arises from combining the Planck-Einstein relation for photon energy with the relativistic momentum-energy relation for massless particles.
photon-momentum-wavelength-relation-de8f.interpretation: This formula, $p = h/\lambda$, is crucial for understanding how light interacts with matter at the quantum level. It implies that shorter wavelength photons (like X-rays or gamma rays) carry more momentum than longer wavelength photons (like radio waves), even though all photons travel at the speed of light. This momentum transfer is responsible for phenomena such as radiation pressure and the Compton effect, providing direct evidence for the particle nature of light. It also highlights the universal role of Planck's constant, $h$, in quantifying quantum phenomena.
photon-momentum-wavelength-relation-de8f.limits_and_boundary: This equation is strictly applicable to photons, which are massless particles traveling at the speed of light in a vacuum. It does not apply to massive particles, whose momentum is given by $p = \gamma mv$. While the de Broglie wavelength extends the concept of wavelength to massive particles, the specific form $p=h/\lambda$ is for photons.
photon-momentum-wavelength-relation-de8f.symmetry_origin: The formula is rooted in the fundamental principles of energy-momentum conservation and the wave-particle duality of light. It reflects the inherent symmetry between wave and particle descriptions in quantum mechanics, mediated by Planck's constant. The constancy of the speed of light, a core tenet of special relativity, also plays a role in its derivation.

operator-product-difference-e5597c56.title: Quantum Operator Commutator Expression
operator-product-difference-e5597c56.description: Defines the Lie bracket or commutation difference $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}$ between two linear operators acting on a Hilbert space. It provides the fundamental measure of non-commutativity and algebraic ordering incompatibility in quantum mechanics.
operator-product-difference-e5597c56.conceptual_definition: The operator product difference $\hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}$ represents the commutator $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]$ on an associative operator algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$. When evaluated on quantum state vectors, a non-vanishing commutator reveals that the observables $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ do not share a complete common eigenbasis, directly yielding the Robertson-Schrödinger uncertainty relation $\sigma_A \sigma_B \ge \frac{1}{2} |\langle [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] angle|$.
operator-product-difference-e5597c56.interpretation: The term $\hat{A}\hat{B}$ denotes the sequential composition of linear operator $\hat{B}$ followed by operator $\hat{A}$, while $\hat{B}\hat{A}$ denotes the reverse sequential composition. The difference measures the algebraic failure of commutativity. If $\hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A} = 0$, the operators commute, implying simultaneous diagonalizability and mutually compatible observables.
operator-product-difference-e5597c56.limits_and_boundary: In the classical correspondence limit $\hbar \to 0$, the quantum commutator $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]$ maps directly to the classical Poisson bracket via the Dirac canonical quantization condition $\lim_{\hbar \to 0} \frac{1}{i\hbar} [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \{A, B\}_{\mathrm{PB}}$. If $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ commute, the expression vanishes identically to the zero operator $\hat{0}$.
operator-product-difference-e5597c56.symmetry_origin: Forms the Lie algebra structure $[\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{g}] \subseteq \mathfrak{g}$ underlying continuous transformation groups (such as rotations, translations, and gauge symmetries) via their infinitesimal Hermitian generators.

\\hat{A}.name: First Linear Operator
\\hat{A}.description: First observable or transformation operator acting on a Hilbert space domain

\\hat{B}.name: Second Linear Operator
\\hat{B}.description: Second observable or transformation operator acting on a Hilbert space domain

operator-product-difference-e5597c56.intuitive_summary: In classical physics, the order of multiplication does not matter. In quantum mechanics, applying measurement or transformation $\hat{A}$ before $\hat{B}$ generally alters the state differently than applying $\hat{B}$ before $\hat{A}$; this expression directly calculates that discrepancy.

transformation-of-vector-time-derivative.title: Transformation of Vector Time Derivative in Rotating Frame
transformation-of-vector-time-derivative.description: This equation relates the time derivative of an arbitrary vector observed in an inertial frame to its time derivative observed in a rotating frame, accounting for the angular velocity of the rotating frame.
transformation-of-vector-time-derivative.conceptual_definition: In classical mechanics, when analyzing motion from a non-inertial (rotating) reference frame, the rate of change of a vector quantity appears different compared to an inertial frame. This formula provides the fundamental kinematic relationship to transform the time derivative of any vector from one frame to the other, specifically when one frame is rotating relative to the other. It highlights that a vector can change both due to its components changing within a frame and due to the frame itself rotating.
transformation-of-vector-time-derivative.interpretation: The term $\frac{d\vec{A}}{dt}$ represents the absolute time derivative of vector $\vec{A} as seen by an observer in a fixed (inertial) reference frame. The term \frac{d' \vec{A} }{dt'}$ represents the time derivative of vector $\vec{A}$ as seen by an observer rotating with the moving frame, meaning it only accounts for the change in the components of $\vec{A} relative to the rotating basis vectors. The term \vec { \omega$} $\times \vec{A}$ is the "transport term" or "fictitious term" that arises solely due to the rotation of the basis vectors of the moving frame. It quantifies how much the vector $\vec{A} appears to change from the inertial frame's perspective simply because the rotating frame's axes are turning. This relationship is crucial for deriving equations of motion in rotating frames, such as those involving Coriolis and centrifugal forces$.
transformation-of-vector-time-derivative.limits_and_boundary: This formula is valid for classical mechanics and non-relativistic speeds. It applies to any vector quantity, provided the angular velocity $\vec${$\omega}$ is well-defined and represents the instantaneous angular velocity of the rotating frame relative to the inertial frame. The rotating frame is typically assumed to have a fixed origin relative to the inertial frame, or the origin's motion is accounted for separately. It is a kinematic relationship, independent of the forces causing the rotation.
transformation-of-vector-time-derivative.symmetry_origin: This equation is a kinematic identity arising from the rules of vector calculus and coordinate transformations between rotating frames. While not directly stemming from a fundamental symmetry like Noether's theorem, it is essential for expressing conservation laws (e.g., angular momentum) in rotating coordinate systems. It reflects the rotational symmetry of space in how derivatives transform.

continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.title: Continuity Equation (Non-Relativistic Local Conservation)
continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.description: Expresses the local differential conservation law for an arbitrary continuous physical density and its associated flux in non-relativistic spacetime.
continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.conceptual_definition: The non-relativistic continuity equation states that the temporal rate of change of a conserved density $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t)$ at a fixed point in space is exactly balanced by the net outflow (divergence) of its spatial flux density $\vec{J}(\mathbf{x}, t)$, precluding unphysical instantaneous action-at-a-distance and ensuring strict local conservation: $\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{J} = 0$.
continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.interpretation: The partial derivative $\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}$ quantifies the instantaneous rate of density change of a conserved quantity $\rho$ at a local spatial coordinate. The divergence term $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{J}$ represents the net outward flux of the current density vector $\vec{J}$ per unit volume. The vanishing sum guarantees that no source or sink exists within the system domain.
continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.limits_and_boundary: In steady-state conditions where $\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0$, the equation reduces to solenoidal flux $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{J} = 0$. In relativistic regimes ($v \to c$), it generalizes to the covariant 4-divergence form $\partial_\mu J^\mu = 0$.
continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.symmetry_origin: Rooted in continuous global $U(1)$ phase invariance (for quantum probability and electric charge conservation) or continuous spacetime translation symmetries via Noether's first theorem.

\\rho.name: Density of conserved quantity
\\rho.description: Local volumetric density of the conserved scalar field (e.g., mass, charge, or probability density)

\\vec{J}.name: Flux density vector
\\vec{J}.description: Current density representing the directional rate of flow of the conserved quantity per unit surface area

\\vec{\\nabla}.name: Del operator
\\vec{\\nabla}.description: Spatial vector gradient differential operator in three dimensions

\\vec{\\nabla} \\cdot.name: Divergence operator
\\vec{\\nabla} \\cdot.description: Vector differential operator measuring the net outward flux of a vector field from an infinitesimal volume

\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial t}.description: Rate of change with respect to time holding spatial coordinates fixed

continuity-equation-non-relativistic-03c.intuitive_summary: Any accumulation or depletion of a physical substance (such as mass, charge, or probability) in a small control volume must be entirely accounted for by the net physical flux crossing the boundary of that volume.

canonical-momentum-and-lagrangian-differ.title: Legendre Transform of the Lagrangian (Hamiltonian Construction)
canonical-momentum-and-lagrangian-differ.description: Defines the fundamental Legendre transformation connecting Lagrangian mechanics on the tangent bundle to Hamiltonian mechanics on the cotangent bundle.
canonical-momentum-and-lagrangian-differ.conceptual_definition: The expression $p\dot{q} - L$ defines the classical Hamiltonian $H(q, p, t)$ via the Legendre-Fenchel transform of the Lagrangian $L(q, \dot{q}, t)$ with respect to generalized velocity $\dot{q}$, where $p = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}}$ is the conjugate canonical momentum.
canonical-momentum-and-lagrangian-differ.interpretation: In this expression, $p$ denotes the canonical (generalized) momentum, $\dot{q}$ is the generalized velocity (time derivative of generalized coordinate $q$), and $L$ represents the Lagrangian of the mechanical system. By substituting $\dot{q}(q, p, t)$ into $p\dot{q} - L$, one obtains the Hamiltonian function $H(q, p, t)$, transforming second-order Euler-Lagrange equations into a system of two first-order Hamilton's canonical equations.
canonical-momentum-and-lagrangian-differ.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit with standard scleronomic constraints, $L = T - V$ and $p\dot{q} = 2T$, simplifying $p\dot{q} - L$ directly to the total mechanical energy $E = T + V$. For singular Lagrangians (where the Hessian $\det\left(\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial \dot{q}_i \partial \dot{q}_j}\right) = 0$), the Legendre transform becomes non-invertible and requires Dirac-Bergmann constraint analysis.
canonical-momentum-and-lagrangian-differ.symmetry_origin: Rooted in symplectic geometry and diffeomorphism invariance of phase space; according to Noether's theorem, if $L$ has continuous time-translation symmetry ($\frac{\partial L}{\partial t} = 0$), $p\dot{q} - L$ is a strictly conserved constant of motion identified with total energy.

magnetic-centripetal-force-balance-8ec31.title: Magnetic-Centripetal Force Balance
magnetic-centripetal-force-balance-8ec31.description: This equation represents the equilibrium between the magnetic Lorentz force and the centripetal force acting on a charged particle undergoing uniform circular motion in a perpendicular magnetic field.
magnetic-centripetal-force-balance-8ec31.conceptual_definition: When a charged particle moves with a velocity perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic Lorentz force acts as the centripetal force, compelling the particle to move in a circular path. This equation equates the magnitude of the magnetic force, which is perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field, to the centripetal force required to maintain this circular trajectory.
magnetic-centripetal-force-balance-8ec31.interpretation: The left side of the equation, $q\omega r B$, is the magnitude of the magnetic force ( $qvB$) where the tangential speed $v$ is expressed as the product of angular frequency $\omega$ and radius $r$. The right side, $m\omega^2 r$, is the centripetal force required for an object of mass $m$ to move in a circle of radius $r$ with angular frequency $\omega$. The equality signifies that the magnetic force is precisely providing the necessary centripetal acceleration, leading to a stable circular orbit. This fundamental balance is crucial for understanding phenomena like cyclotron motion and the behavior of charged particles in accelerators or plasmas.
magnetic-centripetal-force-balance-8ec31.limits_and_boundary: This equation is valid under several assumptions: the particle's velocity is entirely perpendicular to the uniform magnetic field, the particle is non-relativistic, and no other forces (e.g., electric fields, gravity, drag) are acting on the particle. It also assumes a non-zero charge ($q eq 0$), non-zero mass ($m eq 0$), and a non-zero magnetic field ($B eq 0$).
magnetic-centripetal-force-balance-8ec31.symmetry_origin: The magnetic force does no work on the charged particle, implying the conservation of kinetic energy. The circular motion itself exhibits rotational symmetry around the center of the orbit. If the magnetic field is uniform, there is also translational symmetry along the direction of the magnetic field (though this specific equation assumes motion perpendicular to B).

source-position-vector-at-retarded-time-.title: Implicit Retarded Time Equation for a Moving Source
source-position-vector-at-retarded-time-.description: Defines the retarded time $t_r$ implicitly as the emission time along the trajectory $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ of a point source such that an electromagnetic signal traveling at speed $c$ reaches the observation point $\mathbf{r}$ at observation time $t$.
source-position-vector-at-retarded-time-.conceptual_definition: The implicit retarded time equation enforces the relativistic causality condition on the past light cone of a field observer. Because the source is in motion with trajectory $\mathbf{r}'(t)$, the emission time $t_r$ satisfies the transcendental relation $t_r = t - \frac{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'(t_r)|}{c}$. For subluminal motion ($|\mathbf{v}'(t)| < c$), this equation admits a unique real root $t_r$, which establishes the retarded position $\mathbf{r}'(t_r)$ necessary to evaluate the Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields.
source-position-vector-at-retarded-time-.interpretation: In this relation, $t_r$ represents the retarded emission time, $t$ is the current time at the observation point, and $\mathbf{r}$ is the observer's position vector. The function $\mathbf{r}'(t_r)$ gives the source's spatial trajectory evaluated at the retarded time $t_r$. The difference $|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'(t_r)|$ is the retarded Euclidean separation distance between source and observer, and $c$ is the universal speed of light in vacuum. The quotient $|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'(t_r)|/c$ represents the finite signal propagation delay.
source-position-vector-at-retarded-time-.limits_and_boundary: In the static source limit $\mathbf{r}'(t_r) = \mathbf{r}'$, the relation reduces to the explicit retarded time $t_r = t - |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|/c$. In the non-relativistic/instantaneous limit $c \to \infty$, the time delay vanishes ($t_r \to t$). For subluminal velocities $|\mathbf{v}'| < c$, the derivative $\frac{d}{dt_r}[t_r + |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'(t_r)|/c] = 1 - \hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{\beta} > 0$, guaranteeing a strictly unique physical root.
source-position-vector-at-retarded-time-.symmetry_origin: Lorentz invariance and the geometric structure of the Minkowski spacetime past light cone, ensuring causal propagation along null geodesics ($ds^2 = 0$).

z-component-of-gradient-of-scalar-potent.title: Z-Component of Gradient Field from Scalar Potential
z-component-of-gradient-of-scalar-potent.description: Defines the Cartesian $z$-component of an irrotational vector field $\mathbf{F}$ as the partial spatial derivative of an underlying scalar potential $\psi$ along the $z$-axis.
z-component-of-gradient-of-scalar-potent.conceptual_definition: In vector calculus and field theory, when a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is generated by the gradient of a scalar potential $\psi$ (such that $\mathbf{F} = \nabla \psi$), the projection along the orthogonal $z$-basis vector $\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ is given by the directional derivative $F_z = \hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \nabla \psi = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z}$.
z-component-of-gradient-of-scalar-potent.interpretation: The variable $F_z$ represents the $z$-component of the vector field $\mathbf{F}$. The operator $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ represents the partial derivative holding coordinates $x$ and $y$ constant, applied to the scalar potential field $\psi(x, y, z)$. A positive gradient implies the field points toward regions of increasing scalar potential values.
z-component-of-gradient-of-scalar-potent.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the scalar potential is uniform along $z$ ($\partial \psi / \partial z \to 0$), the component $F_z$ vanishes identically. As $|z| \to \infty$, for localized scalar sources, $\psi \propto 1/r$ implying $F_z \sim \mathcal{O}(z/r^3) \to 0$.
z-component-of-gradient-of-scalar-potent.symmetry_origin: Cartesian translation invariance along the $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ direction; gauge freedom corresponds to the invariance of $\mathbf{F}$ under global scalar shifts $\psi \to \psi + C$.

gibbs-entropy-for-discrete-states-3687f4.title: Gibbs Entropy for Discrete States
gibbs-entropy-for-discrete-states-3687f4.description: This formula calculates the statistical entropy of a system in terms of the probabilities of its discrete microstates, representing the average uncertainty or information content.
gibbs-entropy-for-discrete-states-3687f4.conceptual_definition: The Gibbs entropy, also known as the statistical entropy, quantifies the amount of uncertainty or "missing information" about the microscopic state of a system, given its macroscopic properties. It is defined for a system that can occupy a discrete set of microstates, each with a specific probability. This formulation is a cornerstone of classical statistical mechanics, serving as the classical analogue to the quantum von Neumann entropy.
gibbs-entropy-for-discrete-states-3687f4.interpretation: This equation provides a statistical interpretation of entropy, showing that entropy is higher when the system's microstates are more equally probable (higher uncertainty) and lower when the system is in a more defined state (lower uncertainty). It measures the statistical disorder or the number of ways a system's internal components can be arranged while still appearing the same macroscopically. A system with maximum entropy has all its accessible microstates equally probable, reflecting a state of maximum statistical disorder. It represents the average information content per microstate.
gibbs-entropy-for-discrete-states-3687f4.limits_and_boundary: This formula is applicable to systems with a discrete set of accessible microstates. It assumes that the probabilities $p_j$ are classical probabilities, summing to one ($\sum_j p_j = 1$). It is a classical statistical mechanics formula and does not directly account for quantum coherence effects, which are addressed by the von Neumann entropy.
gibbs-entropy-for-discrete-states-3687f4.symmetry_origin: The formula's origin lies in information theory, specifically Shannon entropy, adapted for physical systems by Boltzmann and Gibbs. It reflects the statistical nature of thermodynamic equilibrium, where the system explores all accessible microstates according to their probabilities. It does not directly derive from spacetime symmetries but rather from the statistical distribution of microstates.

second-derivative-of-entropy-with-respec.title: Marginal Thermodynamic Stability Condition for Volume Fluctuations
second-derivative-of-entropy-with-respec.description: Defines the boundary or inflection condition where the second derivative of entropy with respect to volume vanishes, marking the onset of mechanical instability or a thermodynamic critical point.
second-derivative-of-entropy-with-respec.conceptual_definition: In thermodynamic stability theory, entropy maximum postulates require the entropy function $S(U, V, N)$ to be strictly concave with respect to extensive variables. The condition $\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial V^2} = 0$ (or $\frac{d^2 S}{dV^2} = 0$ at constant internal energy $U$ and particle number $N$) defines the spinodal boundary or critical inflection where isothermal/isentropic compressibility diverges, signaling marginal stability between stable ($\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial V^2} < 0$) and unstable (spinodal decomposition, $\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial V^2} > 0$) regimes.
second-derivative-of-entropy-with-respec.interpretation: From the fundamental thermodynamic relation, $\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{U,N} = \frac{P}{T}$. Consequently, $\left(\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial V^2}\right)_{U,N} = \frac{\partial}{\partial V}\left(\frac{P}{T}\right)$. Setting this second derivative to zero indicates that the thermodynamic restoring force against volume perturbations vanishes, which corresponds directly to the divergence of compressibility $\kappa_T$ or $\kappa_S$ at a critical point or spinodal line.
second-derivative-of-entropy-with-respec.limits_and_boundary: As a system approaches a critical temperature $T \to T_c$ or the spinodal limit, higher-order derivatives such as $\frac{\partial^3 S}{\partial V^3} = 0$ and $\frac{\partial^4 S}{\partial V^4} < 0$ govern the criticality and stable universal scaling behavior.
second-derivative-of-entropy-with-respec.symmetry_origin: Convexity and maximum entropy principle arising from the second law of thermodynamics and homogeneity of fundamental relations via Euler's theorem for extensive variables.
